title: Chilapata, Buxa Fort and Jayanti in a week
start: NJP railway station or Bagdogra airport
end: NJP railway station or Bagdogra airport

cost_split.item: Trains and shared cars between bases
Forest lodges and homestays, 6 nights with meals
Chilapata and Jaldapara safaris, jeeps shared by two

meta_description: 6 nights in the eastern Dooars: Chilapata forest, 2 nights at Buxa Fort with the Lepchakha walk, Jayanti's riverbed and Jaldapara rhinos, from ₹21,000 per person.
summary: A week in the eastern Dooars for people who like to walk: a night in Chilapata forest, the stone path up to Buxa Fort for two nights in a Dukpa homestay, two nights on the Jayanti riverbed with the Mahakal cave walk, and a last dawn safari at Jaldapara. About ₹21,000 per person for two. Parks close mid-June to mid-September; check current status before you travel.
intro: Buxa Tiger Reserve fills the corner of the Dooars against Bhutan, and the best of it is on foot. A 5 km stone path climbs from Santalabari through forest to Buxa Fort at 867 m, which guarded a Bhutanese pass, held Indian revolutionaries in the 1930s and sheltered Tibetan monks after 1959. Above it, Lepchakha looks over the whole plain. Jayanti, down on its river, is the base for the walk to the Mahakal cave.

We bookend the walking with forest: a night at Mendabari Jungle Lodge in Chilapata at the start, and a night at Madarihat for Jaldapara's rhinos before the train home. Homestays at Buxa and Jayanti are simple and cheap; the forest lodges cost more. Check current status before you travel.
highlights: Nalraja Garh and elephants in Chilapata
The stone path up to Buxa Fort
Sunrise over the Dooars from Lepchakha
The Mahakal cave walk from Jayanti
A last dawn among Jaldapara's rhinos

days.title: Train to Hasimara, night in Chilapata
days.drive: ≈ 150 km · 4–5 h by train + 20 min by car
days.text: Take a morning Dooars line train from NJP or Siliguri Junction east to Hasimara through tea and forest. A car takes you to the forest corporation's Mendabari Jungle Lodge in Chilapata. In the afternoon, take the Chilapata jeep safari past the brick ruins of Nalraja Garh, an early frontier fort, and along the elephant corridor that links Jaldapara with Buxa. Dinner at the lodge.

days.title: The walk up to Buxa Fort
days.drive: ≈ 45 km · 1.5 h by car, then 5 km on foot
days.text: Drive via Alipurduar's outskirts to Santalabari, at the foot of the hills, and pay the forest entry fee. Hire a porter if your bag is heavy, about ₹500–800. Walk the 5 km stone path up through forest, about two hours with rests, to Buxa village and the fort. Check into a Dukpa family homestay, then visit the fort ruins and the memorial to the 1930s detainees in the afternoon.

days.title: Lepchakha at sunrise
days.text: Leave before dawn with a local guide for Lepchakha, about 4–5 km above the fort, roughly 1.5–2 hours uphill. Watch the sun rise over the Dooars plain, with the rivers shining below. Have tea in the village and walk back down for a late breakfast. Spend the afternoon on short forest walks or sitting in the homestay yard. Ask your hosts about the Dukpa community and their links with Bhutan.

days.title: Down to Santalabari and on to Jayanti
days.drive: 5 km on foot + ≈ 30 km · 1 h by car
days.text: Walk back down the stone path after breakfast; downhill is quicker but harder on knees. From Santalabari, share a car through Rajabhatkhawa to Jayanti, about 30 km. Check into a riverside homestay; ask for a room facing the Jayanti river, which spreads into a wide pale bed of stones below the Bhutan hills. Spend the late afternoon on the riverbed, the best part of any visit.

days.title: Mahakal cave walk
days.text: Walk with a local guide, about ₹600–1,000 a day, up the dry riverbed and through forest towards the Mahakal cave, a limestone cave revered as a Shiva shrine. Local accounts put it at about 5–6 km each way, with some scrambling and river crossings, so wear grippy shoes. Pilgrims crowd it around Shivaratri. Back by mid-afternoon for a rest and a last evening on the river.

days.title: Jayanti to Madarihat
days.text: Share a car west through Rajabhatkhawa and Hasimara to Madarihat. Check into the WBTDC Jaldapara Tourist Lodge or a budget hotel on the highway. Confirm tomorrow's first safari slot at the forest office. In the afternoon, rest after the walking, or stroll the tea garden roads near town. Early dinner; the jeep leaves at first light.

days.title: Jaldapara at dawn, train to NJP
days.drive: ≈ 125 km · 4–5 h by train or bus
days.text: Take the first jeep safari, around 6 am in winter, into the Torsa grasslands, where Jaldapara's roughly 330 rhinos graze in the open at dawn. Back for breakfast, check out and take a midday Dooars line train or a bus west from Madarihat to Siliguri Junction or NJP. Allow a buffer of several hours before an onward train or flight.

includes: Trains NJP–Hasimara and Madarihat–NJP, and shared cars between bases

Find other guests to fill the safari jeeps; four to six people cut each share by half or more.

The Buxa path is steep stone steps in places; wear proper shoes and carry water.

faqs.q: How hard is the walk to Buxa Fort?
faqs.a: Moderate. The path from Santalabari is about 5 km of stone steps and trail through forest, climbing a few hundred metres to the fort at 867 m. Most people take about two hours up with rests. Porters carry bags for about ₹500–800. Children and fit seniors manage it slowly.

faqs.q: What is the history of Buxa Fort?
faqs.a: Buxa guarded a pass on the trade route into Bhutan. The British took it after the Bhutan War of 1865, and in the 1930s it was a detention camp for Indian revolutionaries. After 1959 it sheltered Tibetan monks who had fled to India. Today only ruins and a memorial remain.

faqs.q: Where do we stay at Buxa?
faqs.a: In family homestays in Buxa village around the fort, run mainly by Dukpa families, at about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with dinner and breakfast. Lepchakha above has a few more with a wider view. Facilities are simple; power and hot water are limited.

faqs.q: Is the Mahakal cave walk safe?
faqs.a: With a local guide and in dry weather, yes. The route follows the riverbed and forest, with some scrambling and stream crossings. Do not attempt it in the monsoon or after heavy rain, when the river rises fast. Carry water and wear grippy shoes.

faqs.q: Can we see tigers in Buxa?
faqs.a: Very unlikely. Buxa is a tiger reserve, but tigers are extremely rare there and sightings are almost unheard of. You are more likely to see elephants, gaur, deer, monkeys and many birds. Come for the forest and the walks, not for tigers.

faqs.q: What is the Chilapata safari like?
faqs.a: A jeep drive through dense forest east of Jaldapara, part of the elephant corridor to Buxa. The highlight is Nalraja Garh, the brick ruins of an early fort under the trees. Elephants are often seen. A six-seat jeep with fees costs about ₹2,500–3,500, indicative.

faqs.q: Is this trip good for solo travellers?
faqs.a: Yes, for walkers. Homestays take single guests, and you can often join others for safari jeeps and car shares. Hire local guides for Lepchakha and Mahakal rather than walking alone. Costs per person are higher solo, mainly for cars and jeeps.

faqs.q: When is the best time for Buxa and Jayanti?
faqs.a: October to April, when paths are dry and the rivers low. November to February is cool and clear. March and April are warmer but fine for walking early. The monsoon makes paths slippery and rivers dangerous, and parks close mid-June to mid-September.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit for Buxa?
faqs.a: Indian nationals need no special permit, only forest entry fees paid at the gate or office. Foreign nationals pay higher fees and should carry passports, as Buxa and Jayanti are close to the Bhutan border. Rules change: check current status before you travel.
